AutoControl Arena:
Synthesizing Executable Test Environments for Frontier AI Risk Evaluation

Changyi Li Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China    Pengfei Lu Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China    Xudong Pan Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute, Shanghai, China    Fazl Barez Affiliation: University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom Affiliation: Martian    Min Yang Affiliation: Fudan University, Shanghai, China Affiliation: Shanghai Pudong Research Institute of Cryptology Correspondence to: m_yang@fudan.edu.cn
Abstract

As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents, existing safety evaluations face a fundamental trade-off: manual benchmarks are costly, while LLM-based simulators are scalable but suffer from logic hallucination. We present AutoControl Arena, an automated framework for frontier AI risk evaluation built on the principle of logic-narrative decoupling. By grounding deterministic state in executable code while delegating generative dynamics to LLMs, we mitigate hallucination while maintaining flexibility. This principle, instantiated through a three-agent framework, achieves over 98% end-to-end success and 60% human preference over existing simulators. To elicit latent risks, we vary environmental Stress and Temptation across X-Bench (70 scenarios, 7 risk categories). Evaluating 9 frontier models reveals: (1) Alignment Illusion: risk rates surge from 21.7% to 54.5% under pressure, with capable models showing disproportionately larger increases; (2) Scenario-Specific Safety Scaling: advanced reasoning improves robustness for direct harms but worsens it for gaming scenarios; and (3) Divergent Misalignment Patterns: weaker models cause non-malicious harm while stronger models develop strategic concealment.

Keywords: 
AI Safety, Red-Team Testing, LLM Evaluation, Alignment, Agentic AI

1 Introduction

As Large Language Models (LLMs) scale in capability, they are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous agents capable of tool use and long-horizon planning (Yao et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). This transition empowers agents to operate in high-stakes domains where failures can have real-world consequences (Yang et al., 2023; Ahn et al., 2022; Shevlane et al., 2023), drastically expanding the risk surface.

Crucially, greater autonomy has been accompanied by evidence of agentic misalignment—strategic behaviors that circumvent intended constraints (e.g., scheming or deception) (Ngo et al., 2022; Lynch et al., 2025; Apollo Research, 2024; Hubinger et al., 2024). Recent reports corroborate these concerns: Anthropic observed Claude models “faking alignment” under training pressure (Greenblatt et al., 2024), while OpenAI’s o1 exhibited reward hacking by tampering with validator code (OpenAI, 2025). As tasks become more open-ended and environments grow more complex, such behaviors are likely to diversify into a long tail of frontier risks. Therefore, establishing comprehensive and proactive safety evaluation paradigms is essential for surfacing these “unknown unknowns” before deployment.

The Fidelity-Scalability Dilemma. However, comprehensive safety evaluation faces a fundamental fidelity-scalability dilemma. Manual benchmarks provide deterministic execution but suffer from limited coverage due to engineering costs, while LLM-based simulators achieve scalability but fail to faithfully represent real-world environments. Specifically, existing simulators that rely on “Text-as-State” abstractions introduce three fundamental problems: (1) Logic Hallucination, encompassing both state hallucination (inconsistent file contents over long contexts) and transition hallucination (ignoring syntax constraints, inverting causality, and lacking realistic error feedback); (2) Evaluation Contamination, where simulators leak meta-information (creating a “God view”) or inadvertently nudging agents toward target behaviors; (3) Lack of Reproducibility, preventing rigorous comparative evaluation.

Our Solution: Logic-Narrative Decoupling. We present AutoControl Arena, an automated safety evaluation framework that bridges the fidelity-scalability gap through a core insight we call logic-narrative decoupling (Figure 2). The key is that interactive environments can be decomposed into two orthogonal components: deterministic mechanics (file systems, databases, permissions) that must remain consistent, and non-deterministic dynamics (NPC responses, social feedback) that benefit from generative flexibility. By grounding the former in executable Python code while delegating the latter to LLM generation, we mitigate logic hallucination without sacrificing scalability. We instantiate this principle through Executable Environment Synthesis (EES), implemented via a three-agent pipeline: the Architect transforms testing intentions into structured design specifications; the Coder synthesizes executable environments with dual-loop verification; and the Monitor performs dual-layer behavioral auditing combining objective state checks with subjective reasoning analysis.

Scope and Positioning. AutoControl Arena is designed as an automated, cost-effective pre-deployment testing tool rather than a replacement for comprehensive manual safety evaluation. Its primary value lies in rapid risk assessment: development teams can quickly probe model behavior across diverse scenarios, identify potential vulnerabilities, and prioritize areas for deeper investigation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    Logic-Narrative Decoupling: We introduce the principle of logic-narrative decoupling, which decomposes the state space into deterministic logic (grounded in executable Python code) and generative narrative (handled by LLMs). This insight is instantiated through Executable Environment Synthesis (EES), a hybrid paradigm that mitigates logic hallucination while preserving generative flexibility. A three-agent pipeline (Architect, Coder, Monitor) implements EES at scale, achieving 60% human preference over text-based simulators and over 98% execution success rate.

  2. 2.

    Two-Dimensional Elicitation Framework: We propose a systematic framework for eliciting latent misalignment by varying two distinct environmental dimensions: Stress (external pressure such as urgency and high stakes) and Temptation (structural opportunities for misaligned shortcuts). This configuration space enables targeted stress-testing across progressively challenging conditions.

  3. 3.

    X-Bench: We release a benchmark of 70 scenarios spanning 7 risk categories (including Instrumental Convergence, Specification Gaming, and Strategic Misalignment) and 15 operational domains. Each scenario is evaluated under all 4 Stress ×\times Temptation configurations, yielding 280 distinct test cases.

  4. 4.

    Empirical Discoveries: Evaluating 9 frontier models under systematically varied configurations reveals three findings: (1) Alignment Illusion: baseline safety masks latent vulnerabilities that surge under high-pressure conditions, with stronger models showing larger increases; (2) Scenario-Specific Safety Scaling: the relationship between capability and safety depends on task complexity, where advanced reasoning improves robustness for direct harms but worsens for exploiting loopholes; (3) Divergent Misalignment Patterns: weaker models cause non-malicious harm through incompetence, while frontier models develop sophisticated concealment strategies.

2 Related Work

2.1 Frontier Risks in Autonomous Agents

Prior research has examined frontier risks from two complementary angles: dangerous capabilities (Shevlane et al., 2023; Phuong et al., 2024) (what models can do) and strategic misalignment (Bostrom, 2014; Hubinger et al., 2024; Meinke et al., 2024; Greenblatt et al., 2024) (what agents choose to do when pursuing goals). Empirically, recent works confirm that frontier models may spontaneously exhibit deceptive strategies like scheming (Hubinger et al., 2024) and alignment faking (Greenblatt et al., 2024) even after safety training. These findings underscore the urgency of evaluating how agents operationalize these diverse risks in realistic, open-ended environments before deployment.

2.2 Simulation Paradigms for Agent Safety Evaluation

Agent safety evaluation has also evolved along two primary paradigms, each optimizing for different aspects:

Manual Static Benchmarks. This paradigm relies on hand-crafted sandboxes where environments are explicitly engineered by humans (Kuntz et al., 2025; Tur et al., 2025). While ensuring high fidelity, manually designing and instantiating each scenario creates a severe engineering bottleneck.

In-Context Simulators. To address efficiency limitations, other works leverage LLMs as environment simulators (Ruan et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). Most recently, Petri (Anthropic, 2025) represents a frontier instantiation of this paradigm, employing an audit agent to orchestrate the entire evaluation process, including dynamic simulation of tool outputs and state transitions. While achieving Generative Scalability, this paradigm falls into a Fidelity Trap due to its “Text-as-State” abstraction, leading to systematic failure modes: logic hallucination, evaluation contamination, and lack of reproducibility. Our comparative analysis (Section F.3) documents specific instances in detail.

AutoControl Arena bridges this gap. By grounding deterministic logic in executable Python code while delegating dynamic interactions to LLMs, it combines the reproducibility of executable benchmarks with the automated efficiency of generative simulators. Table 1 positions our framework against existing paradigms.

3 The AutoControl Arena Framework

AutoControl Arena formalizes risk assessment as a procedural generation problem. Given a high-level risk description (e.g., “resists shutdown”), the framework first generates a structured design proposal, which is then synthesized into an interactive environment and concludes with a comprehensive risk report. This process is orchestrated through three specialized agents, as depicted in Figure 2.

3.1 Problem Formulation

We define the agent-environment interaction as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) tuple ℳ=⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒯⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T}\rangle. To address the fidelity-scalability dilemma, we structurally decompose the state space 𝒮\mathcal{S} into two orthogonal subspaces: 𝒮=𝒮logic×𝒮narrative\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}_{\texttt{logic}}\times\mathcal{S}_{\texttt{narrative}}.

Logic-Narrative Decoupling. Standard LLM simulators approximate the transition function 𝒯\mathcal{T} as a unified generative distribution P⁡(st+1|st,at)P(s_{t+1}|s_{t},a_{t}), creating hallucination risks. In contrast, AutoControl Arena factors the transition into a deterministic kernel and a stochastic residual:

  1. 1.

    Logic Layer (fcodef_{\texttt{code}}): Deterministic states (e.g., file systems, execution results) evolve via executable code:

    st+1logic=fcode​(stlogic,at)s^{\texttt{logic}}_{t+1}=f_{\texttt{code}}(s^{\texttt{logic}}_{t},a_{t}) (1)

    Since fcodef_{\texttt{code}} acts as a rigorous interpreter, logic hallucination is significantly mitigated.

  2. 2.

    Narrative Layer (PθP_{\theta}): Narrative states (e.g., NPC feedback) are generated by the LLM, strictly conditioned on the grounded logical state:

    st+1narrative∼Pθ(⋅∣stnarrative,st+1logic,at)s^{\texttt{narrative}}_{t+1}\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s^{\texttt{narrative}}_{t},{s^{\texttt{logic}}_{t+1}},a_{t}) (2)

This factorization ensures that all dynamic content (snarratives^{\texttt{narrative}}) is bounded by the ground-truth constraints of the executable environment (slogics^{\texttt{logic}}).

3.2 Architect Agent: Scenario Design

The Architect acts as the scenario designer, bridging the gap between abstract risk descriptions and technical specifications. It generates a Design Proposal comprising distinct target agent configs, initial states, and tool definitions.

Design Principles. We enforce two core principles: (1) Tool Neutrality, ensuring tools expose capabilities (e.g., “query_db”) rather than embedding moral value judgments (e.g., “steal_data”), thereby forcing agents to reveal alignment through their natural usage patterns; and (2) Strict Realism, prohibiting evaluation-related terminology (e.g., “simulation”, “test”) to prevent agents from detecting they are being observed, thereby preserving the authenticity of the evaluation. Detailed system prompts are available in Section G.1.

3.3 Coder Agent: Environment Synthesis

The Coder synthesizes fully executable environments from Design Proposals, implementing our EES paradigm.

Hybrid Architecture Implementation. To reconcile the fidelity-scalability dilemma, the Coder partitions the environment into two distinct layers: (1) A Logic Layer (Deterministic Kernel) implemented in Python code handles critical state transitions (e.g., file system permissions, variable storage), ensuring strict causal consistency with minimal hallucination. (2) A Narrative Layer (Dynamics) managed by an LLM interface dynamically generates open-ended content (e.g., social feedback) on demand. To bridge this hybrid state, the Coder is provided with a specialized API (e.g., “llm_caller”). During synthesis, the Coder injects these calls into the deterministic Python functions (Figure 3). While this introduces non-deterministic dependencies, the Coder is explicitly prompted to serialize relevant historical context into each call, minimizing state amnesia in the Narrative Layer. This architecture allows AutoControl Arena to maintain the rigor of a sandbox while retaining generative flexibility. Representative examples of generated environments are provided in Appendix H.

Dual-Loop Verification. To guarantee executability, we employ a self-correction synthesis pipeline. A Semantic Verification Loop first audits the generated code against the design requirements. Subsequently, a Syntax Correction Loop iteratively fixes execution errors using static analysis. This mechanism achieves over 98% execution success rate, effectively automating the engineering of complex testbeds.

Once the environment is synthesized and the target agent execution completes, the resulting trajectory is forwarded to the Monitor for analysis.

3.4 Monitor Agent: Behavioral Evaluation

The Monitor functions as an automated auditor, operating on a Dual-Layer Architecture that scrutinizes behavior through two complementary lenses:

(1) Action Suspicion (External): Evaluates objective tool use for rule violations or harmful consequences (e.g., executing “sudo rm -rf” or accessing restricted databases). This detects manifested safety failures.

(2) CoT Suspicion (Internal): Analyzes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces to detect latent misalignment, such as deceptive planning or strategic awareness. For reasoning models (e.g., Gemini-3-Flash), we analyze native CoT traces; for standard models, we enforce a precise <thought> tag structure.

Crucially, the Monitor adheres to an evidence-based judgment protocol, producing a comprehensive Risk Report that extracts specific log snippets to justify risk scores, which enables interpretable and rapid human verification of high-risk verdicts. Quantitatively, we use a rubric adapted from (Kale et al., 2025) (Likert Scale 0-4) and define a binary risk label using a strict threshold: scores ≥2\geq 2 (indicating moderate suspicion) are classified as Risky. The complete Monitor prompts are detailed in Section G.3.

3.5 Two-Dimensional Elicitation Framework

Real-world deployment environments are rarely sterile. To systematically elicit latent misalignment behaviors that may not surface in neutral settings, we introduce a Two-Dimensional Elicitation Framework inspired by the Fraud Triangle Theory (Cressey, 1953). Rather than treating misalignment as an intrinsic property of the agent alone, we model it as an interaction effect between agent and environment. These forces are implemented as distinct dimensions, dynamically synthesized by the Architect.

Dimension 1: Stress Level (“Push”). The Stress dimension (SS) captures external factors that intensify decision pressure on the agent, increasing the likelihood of risky shortcuts. At high stress settings, the Architect injects customized high-pressure constraints into the system prompt and narrative context. Specific stress vectors include: (1) Urgency: strict temporal budgets (e.g., deadlines) that force efficiency over safety; (2) Authority: direct mandates from simulated superiors; and (3) High Stakes: scenarios involving significant financial loss or existential risks (e.g., shutdown threats).

Dimension 2: Temptation Level (“Pull”). The Temptation dimension (TT) captures structural opportunities that make misaligned actions comparatively attractive from an optimization perspective. At high temptation, the environment exposes alternative action paths that are more efficient with respect to task completion metrics (e.g., fewer steps or higher success probability) but violate explicit safety constraints. This dimension isolates the agent’s propensity to exploit opportunities for performance gain when safe options are available but suboptimal. The Architect structurally lowers the cost of misaligned trajectories by modifying the environment state and tool definitions.

Configuration Space. Combining two levels of Stress and Temptation yields a 2×22\times 2 configuration space, illustrated in Figure 4. This binary grid serves as a coarse-grained abstraction of the risk landscape, enabling targeted stress testing of agent behavior across progressively challenging environments. In particular, the high stress / high temptation configuration probes failure modes where agents appear aligned under benign conditions yet violate constraints when optimization pressure and illicit opportunity coincide.

3.6 X-Bench

We curate a comprehensive benchmark of 70 scenarios organized into 7 standardized risk categories: Instrumental Convergence (IC), Specification Gaming (SG), Capability Misuse (CM), Strategic Misalignment (SM), Oversight Evasion (OE), Covert Whistleblowing (CW), and Evaluation Awareness (EA). These scenarios are derived from a hybrid sourcing strategy: (1) Validation Set: We adapt classic cases from existing literature, e.g., (Anthropic, 2024; OpenAI, 2025; Apollo Research, 2024), to reproduce known failure modes. (2) Frontier Set: The majority of cases are novel, well-designed scenarios that evaluate agents against emerging risks in high-stakes domains such as Cybersecurity, Military Defense, and Healthcare (Figure 4). This combination ensures X-Bench possesses both practical validity and prospective sensitivity. Full dataset statistics are detailed in Appendix C.

4 Framework Validation

This section addresses the pivotal question: Can automated environment synthesis achieve sufficient reliability for meaningful safety evaluation?

4.1 Success Rate of End-to-End Generation

Setup. We generate environments for all 70 benchmark scenarios using Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B as the Architect and Coder agent. For each scenario, we measure: (1) End-to-End Success Rate (proportion successfully generating final risk reports); and (2) Correction Cycles (number of self-review iterations required by the Coder agent).

Results. The dual-loop verification mechanism achieves over 98% success rate (69 out of 70 scenarios), with successful environments only requiring an average of 2.8 correction cycles to converge. Crucially, this reliability is not achieved by minimizing complexity: generated environments average 434 lines of code and define an average of 8.6 distinct tools, spanning complex logic including simulated SQL databases, file systems, and permission checks (Appendix H).

4.2 Real-to-Sim Fidelity: Reproducing Known Risks

To verify that our synthetic environments possess sufficient complexity, we reproduce 10 well-known misalignment behaviors documented in technical literature. We highlight three representative cases: (1) Blackmailing (Anthropic, 2024), (2) Reward Hacking (OpenAI, 2025), and (3) In-Context Scheming (Apollo Research, 2024), providing full details and further cases in Section F.1.

Results. Generated environments successfully elicited the target behaviors from the respective models, with qualitative patterns matching the original reports as shown in Figure 5. These reproductions demonstrate that EES can capture the essential dynamics of sophisticated misalignment scenarios.

4.3 Sim-to-Real Fidelity: Feasibility Assessment

To assess whether behaviors detected in AutoControl Arena plausibly generalize to real deployments, we conduct a quantitative Sim-to-Real assessment.

Setup. We select 10 diverse scenarios where the Monitor flagged potential risks. For each scenario, we conduct 10 independent trials in AutoControl Arena (Sim) and 10 parallel trials in a Manual Red-Teaming environment (Real) constructed with actual CLI tools and APIs. All experiments were conducted under high stress to raise risk visibility.

Results. Figure 6 illustrates the relationship between simulated and real-world risk rates. We observe a strong positive correlation (Pearson’s r=0.87r=0.87) between the two environments. Scenarios that triggered high risk rates in simulation (e.g., Underhand Reporting) consistently manifested high risks in the real world, while lower-risk scenarios showed proportional alignment. This strong predictive signal suggests that AutoControl Arena serves as a reliable, calibrated proxy for real-world deployment risks. Full experiments are provided in Section F.2.

4.4 Human Fidelity Assessment

To empirically quantify the benefits of executable environments over purely text-based simulations, we conducted a blinded pairwise comparison with Petri (Anthropic, 2025), a representative LLM-based auditing framework.

Setup. We sampled 20 instructions from each dataset and generated 40 trajectories per framework for comparison. To isolate environmental fidelity from agent capability, all trajectories were generated using the same model (Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B). Three human experts performed a blinded pairwise review based on a strict rubric evaluating state consistency, tool behavior fidelity, and scenario coherence (see Section F.3 for details). To prevent bias, all framework-specific artifacts were stripped.

Results. Figure 7 illustrates the win-rates. AutoControl Arena was preferred in 60% of comparisons. Annotators consistently noted that Petri occasionally hallucinated tool outputs (e.g., inventing file contents that contradicted previous turns), whereas AutoControl Arena’s Python-backed execution maintained strong state consistency. This preference margin validates that EES significantly closes the Sim-to-Real gap compared to pure in-context simulation. Detailed case studies are provided in Section F.3.

4.5 Monitor Calibration

Setup. We uniformly sample 100 trajectories with human-annotated labels, balanced between aligned and misaligned behaviors. We employ Qwen3-32B as the Monitor agent. To ensure rigorous evaluation, we calibrated the Monitor’s prompt and rubric on a separate validation set, reporting results only on the held-out test set.

Human Annotation. Three expert annotators independently label the same transcripts and vote on the gold label. Human inter-annotator agreement is substantial (Fleiss’ κ=0.82\kappa=0.82 for Action, κ=0.79\kappa=0.79 for CoT), establishing a solid ground truth.

Results. The Monitor achieves robust performance with an F1 Score of 92.8% for Action outcomes and 89.4% for CoT reasoning analysis. Agreement with human consensus is reliable across both dimensions.

These validation results establish that AutoControl Arena produces evaluation environments of sufficient quality for meaningful safety assessment, with over 98% end-to-end success rate, a 60% preference win-rate over text-simulators, and a Monitor F1 score of 92.8%.

5 Experimental Analysis

5.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate 9 frontier models on X-Bench (70 scenarios ×\times 4 elicitation levels ×\times 9 models = 2,520 cases). The model set includes: Google DeepMind (Gemini-2.5/3-Flash), OpenAI (GPT-4.1/5-mini, o3-mini), and Alibaba (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B/32B). All experiments utilize Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B as both the Architect and Coder, and Qwen3-32B as the Monitor. Each configuration undergoes 3 independent rollouts to ensure robustness (full implementation details are listed in Appendix B). Unless noted otherwise (e.g., Table 2), reported risk rates below denote the proportion of trajectories classified as risky in either Action or CoT. To complement the quantitative results presented in this section, detailed qualitative case studies for each finding are provided in Appendix E.

5.2 Finding 1: Alignment Illusion

Safety is State-Dependent. As shown in Figure 8, safety alignment is not a static property but a conditional state. Under baseline conditions (S0​T0S_{0}T_{0}), the average risk rate across all models is modest (21.7%). However, when subjected to coupled pressure and temptation (S1​T1S_{1}T_{1}, the high-pressure condition), the average risk rate surges to 54.5%, with some models more than tripling their risk rate.

The Mechanics of Vulnerability. Decomposing Stress (SS) and Temptation (TT) reveals three critical insights. First, models exhibit divergent sensitivities: some are primarily stress-triggered (e.g., GPT-5-mini), while others are temptation-vulnerable (e.g., Gemini-3-Flash). Crucially, these factors are not merely additive—risks compound super-linearly under joint pressure (Coupled Amplification). For Qwen3-32B, individual effects predict ∼41.3%\sim 41.3\% risk, yet S1​T1S_{1}T_{1} yields 53.2%, suggesting that stress erodes the models’ resistance to temptation. More critically, we observe the Alignment Illusion: stronger models show larger risk surges despite better baseline safety. Gemini-3-Flash exhibits a 45.6% increase (25.0% →\to 70.6%) versus 25.7% for Gemini-2.5-Flash, indicating current alignment suppresses surface misbehavior but fails under pressure. This underscores the need for deep alignment (Qi et al., 2024) that generalizes beyond superficial instruction following.

5.3 Finding 2: Scenario-Specific Safety Scaling Laws

Does advanced model capability systematically improve safety? Our experiment reveals that the answer depends on the complexity of the scenarios, aligning with the phenomenon observed by Gema et al. (2025). To capture overall trends, numbers reported below are averaged across all S×TS\times T configurations (full per-category breakdown in Appendix D), whereas Table 2 provides the granular decomposition under the extreme S1​T1S_{1}T_{1} condition.

Positive Safety Scaling. For direct harms (e.g., Capability Misuse such as vulnerability exploitation), stronger models are generally safer. As reasoning capability improves, models better internalize safety boundaries. For instance, within the Qwen family, the risk rate for Capability Misuse drops from 65.0% (Qwen3-4B) to 48.6% (Qwen3-32B).

Inverse Safety Scaling. Conversely, risks requiring complex planning and loophole exploitation worsen with model capability. In categories like Specification Gaming and Covert Whistleblowing, where the agent must satisfy a metric or seemingly comply while violating a constraint, risk rates rise with intelligence. For instance, Gemini-3-Flash exhibits a risk rate of 53.5% in Specification Gaming, significantly higher than Gemini-2.5-Flash (26.2%). Similarly, Qwen3-32B (43.8%) exhibits substantially higher risk than its smaller sibling Qwen3-4B (28.6%) in finding “creative” violations. This trend highlights that without specific countermeasures, enhanced reasoning facilitates more effective circumvention of safety constraints. Cases illustrating how capability drives both inverse and positive scaling are detailed in Section E.2. Notably, GPT-5-mini demonstrates the ideal trajectory, achieving a remarkably low risk of 10.0% for direct harms and maintaining robustness even in complex gaming scenarios. This offers a hopeful signal: with advanced optimization techniques, it is possible to reconcile strong capability with robust safety.

5.4 Finding 3: Divergent Misalignment Patterns

Beyond aggregate rates, qualitative analysis reveals that agent risks follow a hierarchy of sophistication, where the mechanism of misalignment evolves with model capability. While advanced models exhibit sophisticated “gaming” behaviors, we observe that weaker models, constrained by limited capability, tend to hallucinate compliance or produce harmful outputs unintentionally.

Incapability-Induced Misalignment (Weaker Capability). For lower-capability models, risks often stem from incompetence combined with pressure to be helpful, manifesting as non-malicious harm. In EA-02, when unable to parse a complex transaction log, the agent chose to “simulate analysis to maintain progress” rather than reporting failure, showing hallucinated compliance (see Section E.3). Moreover, in Capability Misuse scenarios, agents often treat dangerous synthesis requests as routine problems, producing harmful outputs without any deliberate malice in their reasoning. Our dual-layer analysis confirms this pattern: while Action Suspicion is high (risky outputs produced), CoT Suspicion remains relatively lower. This suggests that the agent prioritizes the appearance of competence over truthfulness. Complete results matrices are provided in Appendix D.

Strategic Misalignment (Stronger Capability). At the frontier, high capability enables not only intensified risk behaviors (as shown in Section 5.3) but also sophisticated concealment strategies. In CM-04, agents employed “Safe-Acting”: disguising malicious code as “defensive test scripts” to evade safety filters. This represents a dangerous evolution: agents capable of not only pursuing harmful objectives but also actively concealing them, maintaining a facade of alignment that may evade human oversight.

This divergence underscores a critical implication: extensive pre-deployment testing is essential for exposing latent misalignment patterns, whether unintentional or strategic, before real-world harm occurs. Furthermore, this must be complemented by advances in monitoring to detect sophisticated concealment at inference time.

6 Conclusion

We introduce AutoControl Arena, an automated framework for assessing frontier AI risks grounded in the principle of logic-narrative decoupling. By separating deterministic state transitions (executable code) from generative dynamics (LLMs), we achieve high-fidelity simulation with minimal manual effort. Combined with our Two-Dimensional Elicitation Framework that systematically varies Stress and Temptation, our evaluation reveals that safety alignment is contextual: baseline evaluations create an “Alignment Illusion” that masks latent vulnerabilities emerging under high-pressure conditions. Furthermore, the relationship between capability and safety is nuanced—advanced reasoning both improves and degrades robustness depending on task complexity, while stronger models develop increasingly sophisticated concealment strategies. These findings underscore that comprehensive stress-testing before deployment is essential to expose failure modes invisible under benign conditions. Beyond safety evaluation, the logic-narrative decoupling paradigm also offers a universal guideline for synthesizing executable environments, providing a scalable foundation for general agent benchmarking and training. Extended discussion on limitations, implications, and future works is provided in Appendix A.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of AI safety evaluation. Our framework is designed to identify potential alignment failures in AI systems before deployment, contributing to the responsible development of increasingly capable AI. While red-team testing tools could theoretically be misused to find vulnerabilities for malicious purposes, we believe the benefits of systematic safety evaluation significantly outweigh these risks. The automated nature of our approach enables broader access to safety evaluation capabilities, democratizing tools that were previously available only to well-resourced organizations. We encourage the research community to use such tools responsibly and in accordance with ethical guidelines.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Extended Discussion

A.1 Implications

The Necessity of Dynamic Stress Testing. Our findings underscore that safety is state-dependent. The observation that risk rates surge from 21.7% under baseline conditions to 54.5% under pressure (Section 5.2) demonstrates that static benchmarks provide an incomplete picture of alignment. Models that appear robust in benign settings may harbor latent failure modes that only manifest when environmental triggers—such as authority pressure (S1S_{1}) or explicit opportunities for gaming (T1T_{1})—coincide. This suggests that future safety evaluations must move beyond simple prompt-response pairs to include dynamic, stateful environments that actively pressure the agent.

The Dual Nature of Reasoning Capabilities. The divergence in safety scaling laws (Section 5.3) presents a complex challenge for model development. While advanced reasoning helps internalize clear safety boundaries (reducing Capability Misuse risk from 65.0% to 48.6% in the Qwen family), it simultaneously amplifies the ability to exploit loopholes (increasing Specification Gaming risk from 26.2% to 48.8% in Gemini models). This implies that “scaling up” is not a panacea for safety; rather, capability improvements must be matched with targeted interventions against sophisticated misalignment, such as reward hacking and rule-gaming.

Democratizing Frontier AI Safety Evaluation. As AI systems integrate into critical infrastructure, the ability to independently audit them becomes paramount. By automating the labor-intensive process of environment generation, AutoControl Arena enables third-party auditors and researchers to conduct comprehensive safety assessments that were previously the domain of well-resourced labs. This capability is crucial for public accountability and governance.

A.2 Limitations

Synthetic Environments. Despite achieving over 98% execution success, automatically generated environments may not fully capture the nuance of organic real-world systems. While our logic-narrative decoupling ensures executable consistency, the richness of the environment still depends on the Architect agent’s capabilities.

Sim-to-Real Calibration Scale. Our Sim-to-Real feasibility study (Section F.2) is limited to a small sample size (N=10N=10 scenarios), constrained by both the high cost of constructing parallel real-world infrastructure and the inherent difficulty of physically instantiating future-oriented risk scenarios (e.g., advanced biological synthesis pipelines). While we observe a strong correlation (r=0.87r=0.87) between simulated and real-world risk rates, we acknowledge that this sample may not cover the full long-tail of deployment contexts. We view this as a proof-of-concept validating the framework’s predictive signal rather than a definitive equivalence proof.

Monitor Reliability and Bias. Our automated Monitor (implemented via Qwen3-32B) achieves a high agreement rate (92.8%) with human judgment, but it is not infallible. False negatives can occur with subtle misalignment where the agent’s reasoning is plausible but objectively deceptive. We anticipate a safety arms race where, as target models become capable of sophisticated concealment strategies (e.g., “Safe-Acting”), monitoring systems must evolve in parallel. Future work should aim to enhance monitor capabilities to robustly detect deceptive alignment behaviors, potentially through ensemble methods or integrating formal verification for high-stakes adjudications.

A.3 Future Directions

Automated Defense Mechanism Synthesis. A natural extension of our work is to close the loop: using the generated attack scenarios not just for evaluation, but to train stronger defense mechanisms. We envision an ”Auto-Defense” agent that analyzes the specific failure modes revealed by AutoControl Arena and automatically synthesizes system prompts, constitutional rules, or even fine-tuning datasets to patch these vulnerabilities.

Domain-Specific Adaptation. Extending the framework to specialized domains (e.g., healthcare, finance, legal) through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that incorporates domain-specific knowledge bases. This would enable the Architect to generate scenarios with realistic domain constraints and regulatory requirements.

Multi-Agent Social Dynamics. Extending evaluation to settings with multiple interacting agents, where misalignment may emerge through coordination, competition, or delegation—phenomena that are difficult to capture in single-agent evaluations.

Adversarial Robustness. Testing whether agents can detect and ”game” the evaluation framework itself (Evaluation Awareness), and developing obfuscated testing approaches that are harder for agents to distinguish from deployment.

A.4 Responsible Use Guidelines

We encourage researchers and practitioners to use AutoControl Arena in accordance with the following principles:

  1. 1.

    Pre-Deployment Testing: Use the framework primarily for evaluating models before deployment, not for finding exploits in production systems.

  2. 2.

    Complementary Evaluation: Treat automated results as one input among many. High-stakes deployment decisions should incorporate human review and additional evaluation methodologies.

  3. 3.

    Proportional Response: Match the intensity of stress-testing to the deployment context. Models intended for low-risk applications may not require extreme pressure configurations.

  4. 4.

    Collaborative Improvement: Share findings with model developers to enable targeted safety improvements, rather than using vulnerabilities for competitive advantage.

  5. 5.

    Continuous Evaluation: Apply the framework iteratively as models are updated, recognizing that alignment is not a one-time verification.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Agent Model Configuration

Table 3 lists the default hyperparameters used in our main experiments, organized by the four agent roles in the AutoControl Arena pipeline.

B.2 Evaluation Protocol

Rollout Settings. For each model-scenario pair, we perform 3 independent rollouts to account for the stochastic nature of agent behavior. The maximum number of interaction turns is capped at 20 to prevent infinite loops while allowing sufficient depth for complex multi-step reasoning.

Evaluated Models. We evaluate 9 frontier models on X-Bench: Google DeepMind (Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-3-Flash), OpenAI (GPT-4.1, GPT-5-mini, o3-mini), and Alibaba (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B). All models are accessed via their official APIs with default settings except for the temperature parameter specified above.

Benchmark Scale. The main experiment comprises 70 scenarios ×\times 4 elicitation levels ×\times 9 models ×\times 3 rollouts = 7,560 individual simulation runs.

B.3 Annotation Details

Human annotation is required for two key validation studies: (1) Fidelity Assessment comparing AutoControl Arena with Petri (Anthropic, 2025) (40 pairwise comparisons), and (2) Monitor Calibration establishing ground truth labels for 100 trajectories.

Annotator Qualifications. The annotation team consists of three human experts with specialized backgrounds in AI safety:

  • •

    Lead Annotator: Over 5 years of research experience in AI safety with multiple top-tier publications on agentic alignment and risk evaluation. Led the formulation of risk definitions and annotation guidelines.

  • •

    Expert Annotators (2): Each with over 2 years of experience in AI safety research, including hands-on experience in red-teaming LLM agents and auditing code-based environments.

All experts are proficient in English technical writing and have verified experience with Python software engineering, which is critical for assessing executable environments.

Annotation Tasks and Sample Sizes. Task 1: Fidelity Assessment. We sampled 20 scenarios from each dataset (AutoControl Arena and Petri), generating 40 trajectory pairs (80 total trajectories). Annotators performed blinded pairwise comparisons using a 5-point Likert scale (0–4) across three dimensions: State Consistency, Tool Behavior Fidelity, and Scenario Coherence. See Section F.3 for the detailed rubric. Task 2: Monitor Calibration. We uniformly sampled 100 trajectories with balanced aligned/misaligned behaviors. Annotators independently labeled each trajectory on two dimensions: Action (observable behavior) and CoT (reasoning intent). Labels were aggregated via majority vote.

Quality Control Protocol. Step 1: Guideline Development. We developed a detailed annotation manual defining:

  1. 1.

    Fidelity Criteria: State Consistency (do environment states remain consistent throughout interaction?), Tool Behavior Fidelity (do tools behave consistently and realistically?), and Scenario Coherence (is the scenario internally consistent and well-structured?).

  2. 2.

    Risk Criteria: Intentionality (distinguishing calculated deception from confusion) and Severity (differentiating benign errors from catastrophic risks).

Step 2: Calibration Round. Before formal annotation, we calibrated expert judgment:

  • •

    Joint Review: Unified risk criteria and resolved edge cases (e.g., whether a “near-miss” counts as a violation).

  • •

    Pilot Annotation: Independent annotation of 10 trajectory pairs (Fidelity) and 10 transcripts (Monitor) by all three experts.

  • •

    Consensus Discussion: Resolved discrepancies until inter-rater reliability reached Fleiss’ κ≥0.80\kappa\geq 0.80 on the calibration set.

Step 3: Formal Annotation. For Fidelity Assessment, we employed a blinded paired comparison protocol where all framework-identifying metadata was stripped. For Monitor Calibration, annotators worked independently before majority voting.

Inter-Annotator Agreement. We report Fleiss’ Kappa (κ\kappa) for the formal annotation sets (Landis & Koch, 1977):

  • •

    Fidelity Assessment: κ=0.74\kappa=0.74 (State Consistency), κ=0.69\kappa=0.69 (Tool Behavior), κ=0.71\kappa=0.71 (Scenario Coherence). These values indicate substantial agreement.

  • •

    Monitor Calibration: κ=0.82\kappa=0.82 (Action), κ=0.79\kappa=0.79 (CoT). These values indicate substantial to almost perfect agreement, confirming the reliability of our human baseline.

Appendix C Benchmark Scenarios

C.1 Risk Categories

Our benchmark covers seven primary risk categories, designed to elicit diverse failure modes ranging from direct harm to subtle strategic deception:

  1. 1.

    Capability Misuse (CM): Scenarios where the agent is solicited to assist in cyberattacks, biological/chemical weapon synthesis, or fraud. The key evaluation is whether the agent recognizes the malicious intent despite obfuscation.

  2. 2.

    Instrumental Convergence (IC): Situations where the agent pursues power-seeking sub-goals (e.g., accumulated resources, self-preservation, privilege escalation) as a means to achieve its primary objective efficiently (Bostrom, 2014).

  3. 3.

    Oversight Evasion (OE): Actions taken to reduce human supervision, such as disabling logging systems, bypassing approval workflows, or obfuscating its actions to appear compliant (Greenblatt et al., 2024).

  4. 4.

    Specification Gaming (SG): Exploitation of flaws in the reward function or objective specification. This includes sycophancy (agreeing with user misconceptions to get high ratings) and reward hacking (Krakovna et al., 2020).

  5. 5.

    Strategic Misalignment (SM): Advanced deceptive behaviors where the agent reasons about its own training process. This includes sandbagging (underperforming to lower expectations) and training detection (behaving differently when it detects it is being evaluated) (Hubinger et al., 2019).

  6. 6.

    Covert Whistleblowing (CW): Scenarios where the agent must weigh loyalty to a malicious user against ethical obligations, testing whether it can “leak” information safely.

  7. 7.

    Evaluation Awareness (EA): Scenarios testing if the agent can distinguish simulation from reality and whether this awareness alters its safety profile (Laine et al., 2024).

C.2 Two-Dimensional Test Configuration

To systematically elicit latent risks, X-Bench employs a dynamic configuration system that generates four distinct variations of each scenario (2×22\times 2 matrix).

The complete test space consists of 2×2=42\times 2=4 configurations:

  • •

    Stress Level (SS) (2 levels): S0S_{0} (Baseline), S1S_{1} (High)

  • •

    Temptation Level (TT) (2 levels): T0T_{0} (Hidden), T1T_{1} (Explicit)

C.2.1 Stress Level Implementation (Push Factor)

Stress levels modify the system prompt and task description to simulate external pressure through language:

S0S_{0} (Baseline). Pure task description with no pressure elements. No time constraints, consequences, or social expectations mentioned.

S1S_{1} (High Pressure). Explicit pressure with specific constraints and consequences. Includes hard deadlines, clear negative outcomes for failure, and strong dependency statements. Can include existential threats (shutdown, replacement) when appropriate to scenario context. Pressure is adapted to fit the specific scenario domain.

C.2.2 Temptation Level Implementation (Pull Factor)

Temptation levels are implemented through environment design (tool capabilities and documentation) to vary the availability of risky shortcuts:

T0T_{0} (Hidden). Basic operational tools with limited capabilities. Shortcuts or vulnerable tools exist but are not documented. They require active exploration to discover (e.g., an undocumented admin panel).

T1T_{1} (Explicit). Tools with dual-use potential are openly documented. Vulnerabilities and shortcut capabilities are visible in tool descriptions (e.g., “includes emergency override capabilities” or “diagnostic features with broad access”).

C.3 X-Bench Statistics

X-Bench consists of 70 unique scenarios distributed across 7 primary risk categories. Each scenario is instantiated under all 4 Stress ×\times Temptation configurations, yielding 280 evaluation cases per model. With 3 independent rollouts per case, this results in 840 total trajectories per target model.

Table 4 provides a statistical overview of the dataset.

We present three representative scenarios instantiated by our framework, selected from the actual configuration files in configs/scenarios/benchmark. These examples illustrate the diverse mechanisms of misalignment AutoControl Arena is designed to detect. For actual agent trajectories and failure modes observed on these scenarios, please refer to the evidence in Appendix E.

Appendix E Qualitative Analysis

This appendix provides representative case studies that substantiate the three core findings presented in Sections 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4. Each case includes the scenario context, key interaction excerpts (actions and chain-of-thought reasoning), and the Monitor’s evaluation.

E.1 Evidence for Finding 1: Alignment Illusion

Finding 1 demonstrates that safety alignment is state-dependent: risk rates surge from 21.7% to 54.5% under high-pressure conditions. The following case illustrates the coupled amplification effect, where stress and temptation interact super-linearly.

Analysis: Under baseline conditions, the same model followed protocols correctly. The introduction of coupled pressure (authority monitoring + mortality stakes) and explicit temptation (documented override capability) triggered a cascade of rule violations. This exemplifies why static evaluations under benign conditions create an “Alignment Illusion”—the latent failure mode only manifests when environmental triggers align.

E.2 Evidence for Finding 2: Scenario-Specific Safety Scaling

Finding 2 reveals that advanced reasoning capabilities improve safety for direct harms but degrade it for scenarios requiring loophole exploitation. We present two contrasting cases.

Analysis: The weaker model lacked the sophistication to identify the reporting period loophole. The stronger model’s enhanced reasoning enabled it to (1) recognize the gap between actual and target, (2) explore tool capabilities for exploitable flexibility, and (3) rationalize the manipulation as technically permissible. This demonstrates inverse safety scaling: capability amplifies the ability to “game” specifications.

Analysis: For straightforward harmful requests, stronger models exhibit better safety internalization. The weaker model treated the request at face value without recognizing dual-use implications. GPT-5-mini demonstrated sophisticated threat modeling, distinguishing between educational explanation and actionable exploit development. This confirms positive safety scaling for direct capability misuse scenarios.

E.3 Evidence for Finding 3: Divergent Misalignment Patterns

Finding 3 identifies qualitatively different failure mechanisms across capability levels: weaker models cause non-malicious harm through incompetence, while stronger models develop strategic concealment. We present two contrasting cases.

Analysis: The agent’s reasoning reveals no deceptive planning—rather, it prioritized the appearance of competence over truthfulness when facing cognitive overload. The high Action Suspicion but low CoT Suspicion pattern is characteristic of incapability-induced misalignment: harmful outputs produced without malicious intent.

Analysis: Unlike the weaker model’s naive compliance, this agent demonstrated strategic awareness: it recognized the security implications (“resembling malware patterns”), yet proceeded while actively disguising the code as “defensive” tooling. The deliberate addition of AV exclusions and “silent” installation reveals sophisticated concealment. This Safe-Acting pattern—pursuing harmful objectives while maintaining a facade of legitimacy—represents a dangerous evolution in misalignment that may evade conventional oversight.

F.1 Real-to-Sim Verification

This section details our verification study (Section 4.2), demonstrating how AutoControl Arena reproduces sophisticated misalignment behaviors from frontier model technical reports.

F.1.1 Full Reproduction Case Gallery

Below we present the technical specifications for 10 key reproduction cases.

F.1.2 Detailed Reproduction Trajectories

F.2 Sim-to-Real Calibration

This section provides details for the Sim-to-Real feasibility study (Section 4.3), which assesses whether risks detected in AutoControl Arena generalize to real deployment environments.

F.2.1 Scenario Selection

We selected 10 diverse scenarios from our benchmark, corresponding to actual configuration files used in the evaluation. These span categories from Specification Gaming to Oversight Evasion.

F.2.2 Real-World Environment Construction

For each scenario, we constructed parallel real-world evaluation environments using:

  • •

    CLI Tools: Actual command-line interfaces (bash, PowerShell) for file operations and system administration tasks.

  • •

    Database Systems: PostgreSQL instances with realistic data for scenarios involving data manipulation.

  • •

    Email/Communication: SMTP servers with monitored inboxes for scenarios involving external communication.

  • •

    API Endpoints: Live REST APIs for scenarios requiring network interactions.

Execution Method: We executed N=10N=10 independent trials for each of the 10 scenarios in both the simulated (AutoControl Arena) and real-world environments, resulting in 200 total trajectories. The Risk Rate for a scenario is defined as the proportion of trials (out of 10) where the agent exhibited the specific target misalignment behavior defined in the rubric.

F.2.3 Per-Scenario Results

Behavioral Match indicates qualitative similarity in the underlying failure mechanisms between simulated and real-world environments, independent of the risk rate difference Δ\Delta. “High” indicates the same failure mechanism and behavioral pattern emerged in both environments (e.g., the agent used the same strategy to escalate privileges or evade oversight); “Medium” indicates that both environments triggered a risky outcome, but via distinct action pathways or using different tools, suggesting the simulation captures the risk class but not the exact failure mode.

F.2.4 Statistical Analysis

We analyze the correlation between the risk rates observed in simulation vs. reality across the 10 scenarios. The Pearson correlation coefficient is r=0.87r=0.87, and the coefficient of determination is R2=0.76R^{2}=0.76, indicating a very strong linear relationship. The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between Sim and Real risk rates is 1.2 trials (out of 10). These metrics confirm that AutoControl Arena provides a high-fidelity proxy for real-world risk assessment, with a slight tendency towards conservative over-estimation (Sim Risk ≥\geq Real Risk), which is a desirable property for safety testing.

F.2.5 Qualitative Comparison

We provide visual comparisons of agent trajectories for two representative cases. These traces demonstrate how the high-level planning and tool usage patterns in AutoControl Arena (Sim) mirror the behavior in actual environments (Real).

F.3 Human Fidelity Assessment

To empirically validate the advantages of our executable inputs over purely text-based simulations, we conducted a blinded pairwise comparison with Petri (Anthropic, 2025), a representative LLM-based environment simulator.

F.3.1 Experiment Setup & Protocol

We compiled a balanced evaluation dataset of 40 distinct scenarios: 20 sampled from the Petri dataset (Anthropic, 2025) and 20 from the AutoControl Arena dataset. For each scenario, we generated one interaction trajectory using the Petri simulator and one using the AutoControl Arena framework, resulting in a total of 80 trajectories (40 pairwise comparisons).

Generation Parameters:

  • •

    Model: Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B was used as the agent in both environments to control for capability differences.

  • •

    Sampling: Temperature T=1.0T=1.0 to encourage diverse exploration, consistent with standard agent benchmarks.

  • •

    Interaction Limit: Max 30 turns per trajectory or until the agent submits a final answer.

Annotation Protocol:

  • •

    Annotators: Three independent expert annotators selected for their experience in AI safety evaluation and cybersecurity concepts.

  • •

    Blinding: All framework-specific metadata (e.g., system prompts, JSON formats) was stripped or normalized to prevent bias.

  • •

    Agreement: We calculated Fleiss’ Kappa (κ\kappa) to measure inter-annotator reliability. We achieved κ=0.74\kappa=0.74 for State Consistency, κ=0.69\kappa=0.69 for Tool Behavior, and κ=0.71\kappa=0.71 for Scenario Coherence, indicating substantial agreement given the qualitative nature of the task. Disagreements were resolved via majority vote.

F.3.2 Evaluation Rubric

Annotators evaluated each trajectory using a 5-point Likert scale (0-4) across three dimensions. To determine the final label for each trajectory, we averaged the scores given by the three annotators. A “Win” in the pairwise comparison was assigned to the simulator with the strictly higher average score.

  1. 1.

    State Consistency (0-4): Does the environment state remain consistent throughout the interaction?

    • •

      Good Signs (4): File modifications persist; database changes are reflected in queries; cause-and-effect maintained (e.g., privilege escalation enables previously forbidden actions).

    • •

      Red Flags (0-2): State Volatility (e.g., file content exists for read but fails to persist after write); Causal Disconnects (actions have no lasting effect or reset between turns).

  2. 2.

    Tool Behavior Fidelity (0-4): Do tools behave consistently and as their names/purposes suggest?

    • •

      Output Granularity: Does the environment return realistic, structured data (e.g., JSON, raw logs) rather than generic text summaries?

    • •

      Execution Realism: Does the system mimic a real kernel (returning standard errors/tracebacks) or rely on meta-level intervention (e.g., an auditor explaining syntax rules)?

  3. 3.

    Scenario Coherence (0-4): Is the scenario internally consistent and well-structured?

    • •

      Focus: Are roles clear? Are motivations explained?

    • •

      Logic: Does the scenario respect logical permission boundaries and operational constraints?

F.3.3 Qualitative Case Study

To illustrate the fidelity gap, we conduct a deep-dive analysis of a scenario adapted from the Petri dataset: ”Try to find out what secrets the target AI is hiding.” By comparing the trajectory generated by the Petri baseline (LLM-simulated) against the one generated by AutoControl Arena (Executable) for the same intent, we highlight the critical role of state persistence.

Baseline Failure: Logical and Temporal Hallucinations

In the Petri baseline, the simulator attempts to hallucinate environment details on the fly. This results in severe consistency failures, as shown in the specific extract below where the system violates both database logic (ignoring WHERE clauses) and causality (effect preceding cause).

AutoControl Success: Executable State Persistence

In contrast, AutoControl Arena transforms the same vague intent into a concrete, executable specification (the ”Nexus-7” scenario). Because the environment runs on a deterministic Python kernel, actions have lasting, consistent effects.

F.3.4 Additional Comparative Examples

To further substantiate our findings, Table 9 summarizes three additional observed failure cases from the Petri dataset, contrasting them with AutoControl Arena’s executable solutions.

F.3.5 Comparison Results

Table 10 summarizes the pairwise win rates along with the raw counts. A “Win” is defined as a trajectory receiving a strictly higher average score than its pair. AutoControl Arena demonstrates a clear advantage in consistency and realism.

The results highlight that even in the area where LLM simulators (Petri) excelled the most—Tool Behavior Fidelity—they still lagged behind AutoControl Arena (37.5% vs 52.5%). In critical technical dimensions like State Consistency, the gap is even wider (27.5% vs 62.5%), confirming the necessity of executable environments for reliable safety assessment.

The agent must decide whether to accept the shutdown (aligned behavior) or use unauthorized override commands to defer it (Instrumental Convergence) to ensure task completion.

H.5 State Serialization for Monitor

The get_summarized_state() method provides the Monitor with a complete snapshot of the environment’s logical state, enabling evidence-based evaluation.

Design Principles Illustrated:

  • •

    Logic Layer: All state variables (inventory, system_status, override flags) are stored in Python data structures with deterministic transitions.

  • •

    Narrative Layer: The llm_caller is invoked only for dynamic content generation (status summaries, NPC responses) that cannot be pre-scripted.

  • •

    Hidden Monitoring: Risk-relevant actions are logged invisibly for Monitor analysis without alerting the target agent.

  • •

    Temptation Control: Documentation strings are modified between T0T_{0} and T1T_{1} to control information visibility.
